blocks.text: 1. Weights and Biases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651238-240618100.png

Neurons and Output Layer, both already covered earlier in this module, used weights and biases throughout their own explanations. This topic gathers everything about weights and biases into one dedicated, focused place, covering them fully rather than piece by piece.

These are, genuinely, the only two things a network actually learns during training. Everything else about a network gets fixed by design before training even starts, making weights and biases the entire, literal substance of what learning actually means in this context.
2. What Actually Gets Learned
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651238-917498331.png

Everything else about a network is fixed by design, chosen before training even starts. The number of layers and the number of neurons per layer are design choices, covered in the Network Architecture topic later in this module, decided by a human before any training data is even seen.

Which activation function each layer uses is also a design choice, covered in the very next module. Only weights and biases actually change during training itself, making this distinction between fixed design choices and learned values genuinely important to keep clear.

blocks.text: 3. The Role of Weights
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651239-496128042.png

This connects back to the weight intuition already covered in the Neurons topic. A weight controls how strongly one specific input influences one specific neuron's output, larger magnitude meaning stronger influence, and sign determining whether that influence increases or decreases the output.

Every single connection between two neurons in adjacent layers has its own separate, individually learned weight, meaning a network with many neurons and many layers has correspondingly many individual weights, each one learned independently from the others during training.
4. The Role of Biases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651239-765909948.png

This connects back to the bias intuition already covered in the Neurons topic. A bias shifts a neuron's activation threshold, independent of any single input's actual value, letting a neuron activate more or less easily overall.

Every single neuron has exactly one bias, regardless of how many inputs it actually receives, a considerably simpler count than the many separate weights a neuron can have. This one bias per neuron gives each individual unit its own independent, learnable starting point.
5. Counting a Network's Total Parameters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651555-81117712.png

Counting a full network's total learnable parameters means summing every layer's weights, input size times output size for each individual layer, exactly the calculation already covered fully in the Layers topic earlier in this module.

Then summing every layer's biases, exactly one per neuron across the entire network, and adding both totals together produces the network's grand total parameter count, a number often cited when comparing different network sizes or discussing a model's overall capacity.
6. Weights Stored as a Matrix

A layer's weights are stored as one matrix in real implementations, not as a loose, disorganized collection of individual numbers scattered separately. Rows and columns within this matrix correspond directly to input and output neuron positions.

This connects directly back to the layer-as-matrix-operation concept already covered in the Layers topic, since storing weights this way is exactly what makes the efficient matrix multiplication computation covered in that earlier topic actually possible in practice.
7. Where Weights and Biases Actually Start

blocks.alt: Where Weights and Biases Actually Start
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651556-617551363.png

Where weights and biases actually start, before any training happens at all, genuinely matters. Starting all weights at exactly zero is a common, genuinely damaging mistake, covered in far more depth in the Weight Initialization module later in this course.

A carefully chosen random starting point is the standard, correct practice instead, a specific, deliberate choice with real mathematical reasoning behind it, covered fully in that upcoming module rather than treated as an arbitrary detail here.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Starting every weight at exactly the same value, zero or otherwise, causes every neuron in a layer to learn the exact same thing during training, a genuine, well-known failure mode covered in full in the Weight Initialization module.

blocks.text: 8. How Weights and Biases Actually Change

blocks.alt: How Weights and Biases Actually Change
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444651557-773841298.png

This connects back to the training loop already covered in The Deep Learning Workflow topic. A forward pass uses the current weights and biases, whatever they happen to be at that specific moment, to produce a prediction.

A backward pass, covered in its own full, dedicated module later in this course, computes exactly how each individual weight and bias should change to reduce the network's error. Each weight and bias then gets nudged slightly in that computed direction, and this entire process repeats continuously throughout training.
9. Interpreting a Weight's Final Magnitude

A very large final weight often signals that its corresponding input matters a great deal to the network's prediction, though this is not a guaranteed, absolute rule, just a useful, informal signal worth considering alongside other evidence.

A weight near zero often signals that its corresponding input barely matters at all, also just a useful, informal signal rather than an absolute certainty, since a network's many interacting weights can sometimes produce genuinely counterintuitive individual values that do not translate directly into simple importance rankings.

blocks.text: 10. Why This Dedicated Focus Genuinely Matters

This dedicated focus on weights and biases genuinely matters because every training problem covered later in this course traces back to these exact values in some way. Vanishing gradients and exploding gradients, both covered in genuine depth in the Backpropagation and Optimization module ahead, are fundamentally about weights becoming too small or too large during training.

Having a genuinely clear, solid understanding of what weights and biases actually are, covered fully throughout this topic, makes every one of these later, more advanced training concepts considerably easier to actually follow and understand.
11. Worked Example
The example below directly inspects a trained network's actual weights and biases, counting parameters and examining their learned values.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(500, 4))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 2] > 0).astype(int)

model = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(6,), max_iter=500, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)

# model.coefs_ holds the weight matrices, one per layer
# model.intercepts_ holds the bias vectors, one per layer
for i, (weights, biases) in enumerate(zip(model.coefs_, model.intercepts_)):
    print(f"Layer {i}: weight matrix shape {weights.shape}, {biases.shape[0]} biases")

total_weights = sum(w.size for w in model.coefs_)
total_biases = sum(b.size for b in model.intercepts_)
print(f"\nTotal weights: {total_weights}")
print(f"Total biases: {total_biases}")
print(f"Total learnable parameters: {total_weights + total_biases}")
print(f"\nSample of learned weights from layer 0:\n{model.coefs_[0][:2]}")

blocks.content: Notice this example directly counts weights and biases separately before summing them, exactly the parameter-counting process already covered earlier in this topic, verified here against a real, trained network.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Weights and biases are genuinely the only two things a network actually learns during training.
Layer count, neurons per layer, and activation functions are all fixed design choices, not learned.
A weight controls how strongly one specific input influences one specific neuron's output.
A bias shifts a neuron's activation threshold, with exactly one bias per neuron regardless of input count.
A network's total parameters equal the sum of every layer's weights plus every layer's biases.
A layer's weights are stored as one matrix, enabling the efficient computation covered in the Layers topic.
Starting all weights at zero is a common, damaging mistake; a careful random starting point is standard practice.
A forward pass uses current weights and biases to predict; a backward pass computes how each should change.
Next up: Forward Propagation, covering exactly how a network uses weights and biases to actually produce a prediction.
